Gross Domestic Product, or GDP. The total monetary value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders during a specific period, usually one year. It's the most widely used measure of a nation's economic size and performance.

GDP can be calculated three equivalent ways. The expenditure approach adds consumption, investment, government spending, and net exports. The income approach sums all incomes earned in production—wages, rent, interest, and profit. The output approach adds value added at each stage to avoid double-counting. All three methods yield the same GDP figure if measured correctly.

There's an important distinction between nominal and real GDP. Nominal GDP is measured at current prices, so it's inflated by price increases. Real GDP is adjusted for inflation using a base year and reflects actual quantity changes, not price changes. Real GDP growth is what economists use to assess true economic expansion.

GDP has significant limitations. It omits non-market activity like household labor and volunteering. It ignores environmental costs like pollution. Per capita GDP—dividing total GDP by population—allows cross-country comparisons and is associated with high living standards. But GDP doesn't measure inequality, sustainability, or happiness. A country could have high GDP but poor income distribution.

The components matter too. Consumption typically comprises sixty to seventy percent of GDP—spending by households on goods and services. Investment is typically fifteen to twenty percent—spending by businesses on capital goods, and it's highly cyclical. Government spending is typically fifteen to twenty-five percent, varying with policy. Net exports complete the picture. If a country imports more than it exports, this is negative and subtracts from GDP.

GDP is the language of macroeconomic policy. Central banks and governments obsess over growth rates because it correlates with employment, tax revenue, and political stability. Two percent growth is considered healthy. Zero or negative growth signals recession and triggers policy intervention. GDP-centrism has drawbacks though. It ignores income distribution, environmental sustainability, and quality of life. Understanding GDP is essential for interpreting economic news and understanding why growth obsession drives much of economic policy.
